fetched_contents.text: Neuraxial analgesia: a review of its effects on the outcome and duration of labor Abstract Labor pain is one of the most challenging experiences encountered by females during their lives. Neuraxial analgesia is the mainstay analgesic for intrapartum pain relief. However, despite the increasing use and undeniable advantages of neuraxial analgesia for labor, there have been concerns regarding undesirable effects on the progression of labor and outcomes. Recent evidence indicates that neuraxial analgesia does not increase the rate of Cesarean sections, although it may be associated with a prolonged second stage of labor and an increased rate of instrumental vaginal delivery. Even when neuraxial analgesia is administered early in the course of labor, it is not associated with an increased rate of Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery, nor does it prolong the labor duration. These data may help physicians correct misconceptions regarding the adverse effects of neuraxial analgesia on labor outcome, as well as encourage the administration of neuraxial analgesia in response to requests for pain relief. Keywords: Analgesia, Cesarean section, Neuraxial, Obstetric labor Introduction Labor pain is one of the most challenging experiences encountered by females during their lives. Painful labor produces maternal physiological changes that may affect maternal and fetal wellbeing. The maternal catecholaminergic surge in norepinephrine and epinephrine in response to labor pain increases maternal oxygen consumption, which may lead to incoordinate uterine action, consequently causing decreased placental perfusion. In some cases, increased maternal oxygen consumption may be deleterious to maternal and fetal health. In addition, maternal hyperventilation in response to labor pain causes adverse effects such as reduced fetal oxygen delivery [1,2]. Besides these acute maternal and fetal hemodynamic and metabolic responses, intense labor pain has been correlated with the development of postpartum posttraumatic stress [3], postpartum depression, and persistent pain [4]. Neuraxial analgesia is the most effective technique for pain relief during labor. Numerous studies comparing neuraxial analgesia with systemic opioids or other techniques have demonstrated the superior pain relief and maternal-fetal physiologic benefits of neuraxial analgesia [5-9]. Furthermore, Hiltunen et al. [10] reported that neuraxial analgesia could reduce the risk of immediate postpartum depression. As a result of the advantage of neuraxial analgesia, its use for labor analgesia has increased continuously over the past several decades. In the United States, the use of neuraxial analgesia has tripled from 22% in 1981 to 61% in 2001 [11]. In recent studies including those of Harkins et al. [12] and the Le Ray et al. [13], the rate of neuraxial analgesia administration reached 75-80% of all women in labor. However, since the introduction of neuraxial analgesia into the labor analgesia field, there has been controversy regarding its effects on the obstetric outcome. While early observational studies suggested that neuraxial analgesia caused a higher incidence of adverse effects on labor outcome, recent evidence no longer supports these historic beliefs. Nevertheless, a number of misconceptions regarding the effects of neuraxial analgesia on the labor outcome still hamper its timely use in obstetric practice. In fact, one of the major reasons offered by patients for refusing neuraxial analgesia is concern about its possible interference with the course and outcome of labor [12,14-16]. Therefore, anesthesiologists should provide correct, up-to-date information regarding the effects of neuraxial analgesia on the labor outcomes for patients seeking labor pain relief. This review summarizes the current research regarding the effects of neuraxial analgesia on labor, focusing on associations between neuraxial analgesia and the incidence of Cesarean and instrumental vaginal delivery, the duration of labor, as well as the impact of the type or administration time of neuraxial analgesia on the outcome of labor. Neuraxial Analgesia and Labor Outcome Observational studies Observational studies are designed such that the researcher naturally observes subjects and measures variables without assigning treatments to the subjects. Therefore, observational studies have high external validity because they reflect actual clinical labor practices without any intervention (no selection bias, no treatment crossover). In early observational studies, neuraxial analgesia appeared to be associated with prolonged labor times and increased rates of Cesarean sections and instrumental vaginal deliveries. These observations developed into a longstanding belief among obstetric providers that neuraxial analgesia delays labor and leads to increased rates of Cesarean sections and instrumental vaginal deliveries. However, interpretation of these studies is complex because of the presence of numerous confounding factors that can adversely affect labor outcome and patient selection bias [17]. For example, patients with complicated labor are more likely to experience severe pain, thus requiring more analgesics. These patients may consequently be more likely to choose neuraxial analgesia than patients with uncomplicated labor. Patients with a complicated labor may independently have a higher incidence of Cesarean section and instrumental delivery. In fact, Hess et al. fetched_contents.text: Fetal heart rate changes and labor neuraxial analgesia: a machine learning approach Abstract Background Neuraxial labor analgesia has been associated with fetal heart rate changes. Fetal bradycardia is multifactorial, and predicting it poses a significant challenge to clinicians. Machine learning algorithms may assist the clinician to predict fetal bradycardia and identify predictors associated with its presentation. Methods A retrospective analysis of 1077 healthy laboring parturients receiving neuraxial analgesia was conducted. We compared a principal components regression model with tree-based random forest, ridge regression, multiple regression, a general additive model, and elastic net in terms of prediction accuracy and interpretability for inference purposes. Results Multiple regression identified combined spinal-epidural (CSE) (p = 0.02), interaction between CSE and dose of phenylephrine (p < 0.0001), decelerations (p < 0.001), and the total dose of bupivacaine (p = 0.03) as associated with decrease in fetal heart rate. Random forest exhibited good predictive accuracy (mean standard error of 0.92). Conclusion Use of CSE, presence of decelerations, total dose of bupivacaine, and total dose of vasopressors after CSE are associated with decreases in fetal heart rate in healthy parturients during labor. Prediction of changes in fetal heart rate can be approached with a tree-based random forest model with good accuracy with important variables that are key for the prediction, such as CSE, BMI, duration of stage 1 of labor, and dose of bupivacaine. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12884-023-05632-3. Keywords: Fetal heart rate, Anesthesia and Analgesia, Machine learning Background Labor combined spinal-epidural (CSE) is associated with rapid onset of analgesia [1]. CSE is associated with increased risk of fetal bradycardia in the absence of maternal hypotension [2]. Although a multivariate analysis revealed that only pain scores and maternal age were independent predictors of fetal bradycardia after neuraxial blockade, there is still controversy regarding the contribution of CSE to this outcome [3]. The mechanism underlying the altered fetal heart rate after CSE with opioids remains elusive; however, uterine hypertonicity secondary to a rapid drop in plasma catecholamine levels may be the culprit [4]. The effect of neuraxial medications on fetal heart rate is poorly understood. It is unknown whether any differences in risk exist between fentanyl and bupivacaine when used in CSE procedures. There are reports of uterine hyperactivity and fetal bradycardia following subarachnoid administration of fentanyl during labor [5]. Given the multifactorial nature of changes in fetal heart rate during labor, our study aims to perform statistical inference and prediction of changes in fetal heart rate during active labor in healthy pregnant women by comparing three different machine learning methods: multiple linear regression, splines, and elastic lasso. We aim to identify the contribution of different predictive factors to changes in fetal heart rate in the context of normal labor and create an accurate model to predict those changes in future parturients scheduled for vaginal delivery. Methods This study has been reported according to the STROBE guidelines [6]. According to the Declaration of Helsinki was registered at https://clinicaltrials.gov/, under the registration code NCT05399979. After approval by the Augusta University Committee A Review Board (Protocol #: 1,567,908. 03/16/2021), a retrospective chart review was conducted for healthy parturients admitted for vaginal delivery between November 2017 and August 2020. In agreement with the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA), we defined healthy pregnant patients as an ASA Physical Status Classification system II [7]. Information for the study was obtained from the institutional electronic information system of Augusta University Medical Center. Patients older than 18 years old with healthy term pregnancies (> 37 weeks) were included. Patients with baseline systolic blood pressure < 90 and diastolic blood pressure < 60, maternal fever, and uterine tachysystole > 5 contractions in 10 min before neuraxial block were excluded. Also, patients with American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) category III fetal heart rate tracing were excluded. After neuraxial block, a wedge was placed under the patient and adequate hydration was ensured as preventive measures. The dataset was de-identified after the data collection. Mini-report on the evidence for association

The evidence base for an association between neuraxial analgesia and instrumental vaginal delivery is mixed and partly inconsistent across study designs. The strongest direct support comes from observational studies and meta-analyses, but these findings are often tempered by confounding and study limitations. In the provided evidence, a 2011 meta-analysis is explicitly cited as demonstrating that neuraxial labor analgesia was associated with an increased risk of instrumental vaginal birth, with a relative risk of 1.42 (95% CI not fully visible in the excerpt) [N1-R1]. Another meta-analysis in the same review context is referenced as part of the broader evidence base on the topic [N1-R5]. The review itself states that early observational studies suggested neuraxial analgesia was associated with prolonged labor times and increased rates of Cesarean sections and instrumental vaginal deliveries, but that these findings were difficult to interpret because of confounding factors and patient selection bias [N1-F1].

For cohort studies, the evidence is more limited in the provided excerpts. One cited source mentions that a meta-analysis including over 86,000 participants and multiple prospective cohort studies observed significantly decreased rates of PPD (postpartum depression) [N1-R4], but this is not directly relevant to instrumental vaginal delivery. A separate source notes that a meta-analysis of 11 trials comparing PIEB+PCEA with CEI+PCEA found a lower rate of assisted vaginal delivery with the former, but the excerpt does not specify whether this is neuraxial analgesia or a different analgesia regimen [N1-R3]. This suggests that the instrumental delivery literature is partly shaped by different analgesia regimens and that the association may not be universal across analgesia types.

Subgroup findings and dose-response patterns are also present, though the evidence in the provided excerpts is not exhaustive. The review mentions that observational studies are designed to reflect actual clinical labor practices and may therefore have high external validity, but they are still limited by confounding and selection bias [N1-F1]. The JAMA Network Open state-level variation study is cited as performing subgroup analysis by mode of delivery, which implies that subgroup findings can be used to examine whether neuraxial analgesia use varies by delivery type, but the excerpt does not report the exact subgroup results for instrumental vaginal delivery [N4-F2]. The Cochrane review excerpt from the shared dependencies indicates that neuraxial labor analgesia increased the rate of instrumental deliveries compared to non-NLA, with a relative risk of 1.42 (95% CI 1.28–1.57) [N3-R2], which supports the idea that subgroup findings can be consistent across reviews. However, the evidence does not provide a clear dose-response gradient in the excerpts provided.

Overall, the strength of evidence across designs is uneven. The 2011 meta-analysis and the Cochrane review excerpt provide direct support for an increased risk of instrumental vaginal delivery [N1-R1][N3-R2], but they are not the only relevant evidence. The review also notes that observational studies are not capable of reliably indicating whether neuraxial analgesia increases the risk of Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery [N3-R1], which indicates that observational evidence is suggestive but not definitive. Cohort studies and meta-analyses are therefore important, but they are subject to the same limitations and should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N1-R4].

Mini-report on confounding and study limitations

The main confounders and limitations in the evidence are substantial. The review explicitly identifies labor duration, fetal distress, and indication for analgesia as important confounders [N1-F1]. It explains that patients with complicated labor are more likely to experience severe pain and thus require more analgesics, and that these patients may also be more likely to choose neuraxial analgesia than women with uncomplicated labor [N1-F1]. This is a classic indication bias: the request for analgesia may reflect underlying risk factors for adverse outcomes rather than being a direct cause of them. The review also notes that patients with complicated labor may independently have a higher incidence of Cesarean section and instrumental delivery, so any association between analgesia and delivery mode could be explained by the underlying labor complications rather than the analgesia itself [N1-F1].

Selection bias is another major limitation. The review says that observational studies are designed to observe subjects naturally and therefore have high external validity, but this does not eliminate selection bias in the sense that the sample may not be representative of a homogeneous population [N1-F1]. More importantly, the review states that observational studies are not capable of reliably indicating whether neuraxial analgesia increases the risk of Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery [N3-R1]. This is because the observed association can be confounded by unmeasured or imbalanced covariates, including maternal characteristics, labor management, and fetal status.

The provided evidence also highlights the importance of subgroup analysis and study setting. The JAMA Network Open state-level variation study is cited as performing subgroup analysis by mode of delivery, indicating that findings may vary by delivery type and population setting [N4-F2]. This supports the idea that the association may not be uniform across all populations. The review further notes that neuraxial analgesia use varies by state and by delivery mode, and that subgroup analysis can help examine prevalence differences [N4-F2]. This implies that findings are setting-dependent and that generalizing across populations may be premature.

By analgesia type, the evidence suggests that the association may not be uniform. The Cochrane review excerpt references neuraxial labor analgesia compared to non-NLA, but it does not specify whether all neuraxial techniques are equivalent [N3-R2]. The review also notes that neuraxial analgesia is a broad category that may include different techniques, and that study designs can differ in how they classify analgesia and measure outcomes [N1-F1]. The provided evidence therefore supports the conclusion that findings may vary by analgesia type, study setting, and subgroup, making the association context-sensitive.

In summary, the main confounders are labor duration, fetal distress, and indication for analgesia, and the main study limitations are selection bias, indication bias, and the difficulty of isolating a true causal effect in observational studies [N1-F1][N3-R1]. Subgroup analysis by delivery mode and state-level variation suggest that findings may differ by population, setting, and analgesia type [N4-F2].

Mini-report on alternative interpretations and evidence gaps

Alternative interpretations for the association between neuraxial analgesia and instrumental vaginal delivery include the idea that pain relief may reduce spontaneous maternal effort, thereby affecting labor progression and the need for instrumental delivery. The evidence in the provided excerpts does not directly state this mechanism, but it does support a broader interpretation that maternal pain and analgesia are part of a dynamic physiological process that can influence labor outcomes [N1-F1]. The review notes that intense labor pain correlates with postpartum depression and persistent pain, and that neuraxial analgesia is used because it offers superior pain relief and maternal-fetal physiologic benefits [N1-F1]. This implies that pain relief is not merely a passive treatment but may alter maternal behavior and effort during labor.

Observational studies may overestimate or underestimate the association for several reasons. The review explicitly states that observational studies are not capable of reliably indicating whether neuraxial analgesia increases the risk of Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery [N3-R1]. This is because observational designs are vulnerable to confounding and indication bias, and because the request for analgesia may itself be a marker of higher-risk labor rather than a direct cause of adverse outcomes [N1-F1]. The review also notes that early observational studies suggested prolonged labor and increased rates of adverse outcomes, but recent evidence no longer supports these historic beliefs [N1-F1]. This suggests that observational findings can be misleading and that they should be interpreted alongside more rigorous studies.

On the other hand, observational studies may underestimate the association if the true effect is small and masked by confounding or if the study population is not representative. The review says that observational studies have high external validity because they reflect actual clinical labor practices, but it also says they are limited by confounding and selection bias [N1-F1]. This means that they can capture real-world patterns but are not the best tools for establishing causality. The provided evidence also highlights that subgroup analysis by mode of delivery is important, suggesting that findings may vary and that the association may be stronger or weaker in certain subgroups [N4-F2].

What remains uncertain or inconsistent across studies is the magnitude and direction of the association. The meta-analysis cited in the evidence reports an increased risk of instrumental vaginal delivery (RR 1.42) [N1-R1], while other sources suggest that neuraxial analgesia does not significantly increase the risk of Cesarean delivery, with a relative risk of 1.07 (95% CI not fully visible in the excerpt) [N5-R5]. This inconsistency between instrumental delivery and Cesarean delivery indicates that the association is not uniform across outcomes. The review also notes that much evidence suggests neuraxial analgesia does not increase the frequency of Cesarean sections in comparison to systemic opioids [N4-R1], which further underscores the need for careful interpretation.

Overall, the evidence suggests that alternative explanations such as reduced spontaneous maternal effort and pain-related behavior changes are plausible, while observational studies are likely to overestimate or underestimate the association because of confounding, indication bias, and study design limitations [N1-F1][N3-R1]. The evidence remains uncertain and inconsistent across studies, especially when comparing instrumental vaginal delivery, Cesarean delivery, and different analgesia types [N1-R1][N4-R1][N5-R5].

Mini-report on mechanistic explanations

The mechanistic evidence points to several biological and physiological pathways that may link neuraxial analgesia to instrumental vaginal delivery. The strongest direct evidence is fetal heart rate changes and uterine hypertonus. A fetal heart rate study explicitly states that fetal bradycardia has been observed after neuraxial labor analgesia via a mechanism involving uterine hypertonus mediated by catecholamine responses [N2-R1]. Another source reports that initiation of neuraxial anesthesia has been associated with fetal heart rate abnormalities, including bradycardia, reduced variability, and decelerations [N2-R2]. A third source similarly notes that intrathecal medication administration can cause transient maternal hypotension, itching, or a decrease in fetal heart rate (FHR) [N6-R3]. Together, these sources support a biological pathway in which neuraxial analgesia may alter maternal-fetal physiology, particularly through catecholamine-mediated uterine hypertonus and direct effects on fetal heart rate [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3].

A second physiological pathway is reduced maternal pushing or altered labor dynamics. The review notes that neuraxial analgesia is the mainstay analgesic for intrapartum pain relief and that it may reduce maternal stress responses [N3-R4]. It also states that neuraxial analgesia may reduce stress responses to delivery, which could affect subsequent neurodevelopmental outcomes [N3-R4]. Although this excerpt does not directly discuss instrumental delivery, it implies that analgesia may reduce maternal effort and change labor dynamics by dampening the physiological stress response. The review also emphasizes that neuraxial analgesia is associated with prolonged second-stage labor and increased rate of instrumental vaginal delivery, while not increasing Cesarean section [N1-F1]. This suggests that the analgesic effect may prolong labor and reduce maternal spontaneous pushing, making instrumental delivery more likely [N1-F1].

Analgesia timing may also affect fetal and maternal responses. The review notes that early neuraxial analgesia does not increase Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery and does not prolong labor duration [N1-F1]. This indicates that timing is a critical variable: early versus late administration may have different effects on labor progression and outcomes. The evidence also suggests that the relationship between analgesia and fetal heart rate changes is not uniform; for example, the machine learning study found that combined spinal-epidural (CSE) and vasopressor use were associated with decreased fetal heart rate, while pain scores and maternal age were independent predictors [N2-F3]. This implies that the timing and type of analgesia, along with concomitant medications, can influence fetal responses [N2-F3].

Taken together, the mechanistic explanations are plausible but not fully established. The evidence supports fetal heart rate changes and uterine hypertonus as biological pathways, reduced maternal pushing and altered labor dynamics as physiological pathways, and analgesia timing as a modifying factor that can affect fetal and maternal responses [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3][N3-R4][N1-F1]. However, the evidence is heterogeneous and partly observational, so causality remains uncertain [N3-R1].

Although this excerpt does not directly discuss instrumental delivery, it implies that analgesia may reduce maternal effort and change labor dynamics by dampening the physiological stress response. The review also emphasizes that neuraxial analgesia is associated with prolonged second-stage labor and an increased rate of instrumental vaginal delivery, while not increasing Cesarean section [N1-F1]. This suggests that the analgesic effect may prolong labor and reduce maternal spontaneous pushing, making instrumental delivery more likely [N1-F1].

### Analgesia timing and modifying factors

Analgesia timing may also affect fetal and maternal responses. The review notes that early neuraxial analgesia does not increase Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery and does not prolong labor duration [N1-F1]. This indicates that timing is a critical variable: early versus late administration may have different effects on labor progression and outcomes. The evidence also suggests that the relationship between analgesia and fetal heart rate changes is not uniform; for example, the machine learning study found that combined spinal-epidural (CSE) and vasopressor use were associated with decreased fetal heart rate, while pain scores and maternal age were independent predictors [N2-F3]. This implies that the timing and type of analgesia, along with concomitant medications, can influence fetal responses [N2-F3].

## 3) Why the association is not straightforward

### Confounding and study design limitations

The association is not straightforward because of major confounding and study design limitations. The review explicitly identifies labor duration, fetal distress, and indication for analgesia as important confounders [N1-F1]. It explains that patients with complicated labor are more likely to experience severe pain and thus require more analgesics, and that these patients may also be more likely to choose neuraxial analgesia than women with uncomplicated labor [N1-F1]. This is a classic indication bias: the request for analgesia may reflect underlying risk factors for adverse outcomes rather than being a direct cause of them. The review also notes that patients with complicated labor may independently have a higher incidence of Cesarean section and instrumental delivery, so any association between analgesia and delivery mode could be explained by the underlying labor complications rather than the analgesia itself [N1-F1].

Selection bias is another major limitation. The review says observational studies are designed to observe subjects naturally and therefore have high external validity, but this does not eliminate selection bias in the sense that the sample may not be representative of a homogeneous population [N1-F1]. More importantly, the review states that observational studies are not capable of reliably indicating whether neuraxial analgesia increases the risk of Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery [N3-R1]. This is because observational designs are vulnerable to confounding and indication bias, and because the request for analgesia may itself be a marker of higher-risk labor rather than a direct cause of adverse outcomes [N1-F1].

### Population-specific and subgroup variation

The evidence also suggests that findings may vary by population, setting, and analgesia type. The JAMA Network Open state-level variation study is cited as performing subgroup analysis by mode of delivery, indicating that findings may vary by delivery type and population setting [N4-F2]. This supports the idea that the association is not uniform across all populations. The review further notes that neuraxial analgesia use varies by state and by delivery mode, and that subgroup analysis can help examine prevalence differences [N4-F2]. This implies that findings are setting-dependent and that generalizing across populations may be premature.

By analgesia type, the evidence suggests the association may not be uniform. The Cochrane review excerpt references neuraxial labor analgesia compared to non-NLA, but it does not specify whether all neuraxial techniques are equivalent [N3-R2]. The review also notes that neuraxial analgesia is a broad category that may include different techniques, and that study designs can differ in how they classify analgesia and measure outcomes [N1-F1]. The provided evidence therefore supports the conclusion that findings may vary by analgesia type, study setting, and subgroup, making the association context-sensitive [N1-F1][N4-F2].

## 4) Alternative interpretations and evidence gaps

Alternative interpretations for the association include the idea that pain relief may reduce spontaneous maternal effort, thereby affecting labor progression and the need for instrumental delivery. The evidence in the provided excerpts does not directly state this mechanism, but it does support a broader interpretation that maternal pain and analgesia are part of a dynamic physiological process that can influence labor outcomes [N1-F1]. The review notes that intense labor pain correlates with postpartum depression and persistent pain, and that neuraxial analgesia is used because it offers superior pain relief and maternal-fetal physiologic benefits [N1-F1]. This implies that pain relief is not merely a passive treatment but may alter maternal behavior and effort during labor.

Observational studies may overestimate or underestimate the association for several reasons. The review explicitly states that observational studies are not capable of reliably indicating whether neuraxial analgesia increases the risk of Cesarean section or instrumental vaginal delivery [N3-R1]. This is because observational designs are vulnerable to confounding and indication bias, and because the request for analgesia may itself be a marker of higher-risk labor rather than a direct cause of adverse outcomes [N1-F1]. The review also notes that early observational studies suggested prolonged labor and increased rates of adverse outcomes, but recent evidence no longer supports these historic beliefs [N1-F1]. This suggests that observational findings can be misleading and that they should be interpreted alongside more rigorous studies.

On the other hand, observational studies may underestimate the association if the true effect is small and masked by confounding or if the study population is not representative. The review says observational studies have high external validity because they reflect actual clinical labor practices, but it also says they are limited by confounding and selection bias [N1-F1]. This means that they can capture real-world patterns but are not the best tools for establishing causality. The provided evidence also highlights that subgroup analysis by mode of delivery is important, suggesting that findings may vary and that the association may be stronger or weaker in certain subgroups [N4-F2].

## 5) What remains uncertain or inconsistent

What remains uncertain or inconsistent across studies is the magnitude and direction of the association. The meta-analysis cited in the evidence reports an increased risk of instrumental vaginal delivery (RR 1.42) [N1-R1], while other sources suggest that neuraxial analgesia does not significantly increase the risk of Cesarean delivery, with a relative risk of 1.07 (95% CI not fully visible in the excerpt) [N5-R5]. This inconsistency between instrumental delivery and Cesarean delivery indicates that the association is not uniform across outcomes. The review also notes that much evidence suggests neuraxial analgesia does not increase the frequency of Cesarean sections in comparison to systemic opioids [N4-R1], which further underscores the need for careful interpretation.

In short, the evidence supports an association between neuraxial analgesia and increased instrumental vaginal delivery, but the association is not uniform and should be interpreted cautiously. The proposed explanations include fetal heart rate changes and uterine hypertonus, reduced maternal pushing or altered labor dynamics, and analgesia timing as a modifying factor [N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R3][N3-R4][N1-F1]. At the same time, confounding, indication bias, and study design limitations make the causal inference uncertain [N1-F1][N3-R1]. Subgroup findings and population-specific variation further suggest that the association depends on context, analgesia type, and delivery setting [N4-F2][N3-R2].
